standard.title: Analyse civic perspectives
standard.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have analysed civic information at Year 7 level (AC9HC7S03) to identify differences in perspectives. The gap this descriptor fills is the move to analysis that also identifies and explains potential challenges — not just that perspectives differ, but why they differ and what consequences those differences have for civic and democratic life.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges, drawing on a range of source types including speeches, award criteria, letters and case studies.

nodes.label: Identifying differences in perspective
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify differences in perspective in information about a civic issue, explaining what the perspectives are and naming the values or interests that ground them.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different perspectives on a civic issue from provided information and explain what grounds each perspective.
nodes.typical_width: Examine information from multiple sources on a civic issue — such as letters to the editor about a current issue or perspectives on marriage equality — identifying the different perspectives represented, naming the values or interests that ground each perspective, and explaining the key differences between them.
wider: Investigate how the same civic issue (e.g. immigration, climate policy, Indigenous rights) is framed differently across a range of source types — news, advocacy, government, academic — and explain how each framing reflects a distinct perspective
Examine speeches from prominent Australian politicians or jurists on the same issue and identify the values and assumptions that produce different positions

Practise perspective-mapping: systematically recording all identified perspectives on a civic issue with their grounding values, and then identifying patterns (e.g. which perspectives dominate, which are marginalised)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students can identify perspectives but cannot explain what grounds them (values, interests, experiences), their analysis remains superficial and they cannot reason about why potential challenges arise. The grounding of perspectives is the key analytical move that enables the rest of this descriptor.

response_modes.reason: Students often describe perspectives as 'Person A thinks X, Person B thinks Y' without explaining why. Invest in the reasoning scaffold: what values, experiences or interests produce each position, and how do those differences explain the disagreement?

success_criteria: Can identify at least two different perspectives on a civic issue
Can explain at least one value or interest that grounds each perspective, not just describe what each person believes

nodes.label: Explaining reasons for perspective differences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain possible reasons for differences in perspective about a civics and citizenship issue — connecting perspective differences to underlying values, experiences, roles or positions.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two possible reasons why perspectives on a civic issue differ, grounded in the specific issue being examined.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain possible reasons for differences in perspectives on a civic issue — such as marriage equality — drawing on factors such as religious beliefs, cultural background, lived experience, political ideology, professional role (e.g. politician, jurist, advocate) or personal interest.
wider: Investigate how power relationships affect whose perspectives are heard in civic debate — examining why some perspectives are more prominent in official discourse than others

Examine how the same individual can hold different perspectives in different roles (e.g. as a politician vs as a parent vs as a member of a faith community) and what this reveals about the complexity of civic perspective

Analyse the Australian of the Year and Young Australian of the Year criteria and the different ways recipients have met them — examining how different expressions of 'good citizenship' reflect different values and priorities

response_modes.reason: Reasons for perspective differences vary significantly by issue type. Widening across different civic contexts — legal issues, identity issues, political issues — builds transferable analytical skill.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Understanding why perspectives differ — not just that they do — is a critical thinking skill with broad civic application. Width across different issue contexts and different types of perspective-grounding factors builds robust analytical capability.
success_criteria: Can explain at least two reasons why perspectives on a specific civic issue differ
Can connect each reason to specific features of the issue or the perspectives involved

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining potential challenges
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify potential challenges arising from perspective differences on civic issues and explain what makes those challenges significant for civic and democratic life.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one potential challenge that arises from perspective differences on a civic issue and explain why it is a challenge.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a civic issue to identify potential challenges arising from perspective differences — such as challenges to democratic decision-making, social cohesion, legal interpretation or policy implementation — and explain what makes those challenges significant and what is at stake.
wider: Investigate how Australian democratic institutions manage perspective conflicts (e.g. parliamentary debate, judicial review, public consultation) and evaluate how effective each mechanism is
Examine a civic issue where perspective differences have led to a genuine democratic challenge (e.g. a referendum, a contested court decision) and analyse how the challenge played out
Investigate how mediation, negotiation and consensus-building mechanisms work in civic contexts — and what conditions make them more or less likely to succeed

response_modes.reason: Identifying potential challenges integrates perspective identification and explanation into an evaluative judgment about consequences. This is the full demand of the descriptor — ensure students connect all three analytical moves: identify perspectives, explain their grounds, identify what challenges they create.

success_criteria: Can identify at least one potential challenge arising from perspective differences on a civic issue
Can explain why that challenge matters for civic or democratic life, not just describe it
